title: Zelenskyy Offers 'Energy Truce' with Russia — But Can It Hold?
summary:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says his country is ready for an 'energy ceasefire' with Russia — a deal where both sides stop attacking each other's power and fuel systems. He made the offer after a 40-minute meeting with US President Donald Trump in New York, where both leaders were attending the UN General Assembly.

'Both the US and Ukraine want to see this senseless Russian war ended before winter,' Zelenskyy wrote on X. He said the talks were 'positive and productive.'

The idea is simple: if Russia stops targeting Ukraine's electricity, heating, and water supplies, Ukraine will stop attacking Russian oil refineries and fuel depots. 'We are ready for energy ceasefire,' Zelenskyy told reporters.

But there's a catch. Just last week, the two countries agreed to stop hitting each other's energy facilities — and the strikes resumed almost immediately. Zelenskyy also warned on Telegram that Russia is preparing 'a new massive attack' against Ukraine.

The stakes are high. Russia has repeatedly pounded Ukraine's power and port infrastructure. On September 15, Russia launched about 200 drones across Ukraine, hitting petrol stations in Kyiv. Ukraine has fought back with long-range drones that struck refineries up to 3,000 kilometers (1,860 miles) away. A September 20 attack forced Moscow's oil refinery — which processed about 230,000 barrels of crude a day — to halt processing.

Trump is worried about the global economy: he says Ukraine's strikes are driving up diesel prices, which could hurt his party in November's US midterm elections. But Zelenskyy insists there can be no talk of easing sanctions on Russia while Ukrainians live under daily threat of missile and drone attacks.

Zelenskyy also asked Trump for more Patriot air-defense missiles — the only weapon Ukraine has that can shoot down Russia's ballistic missiles. But global supplies are depleted because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

So the question remains: can an energy truce actually hold this time, or will winter bring more attacks?
why_it_matters: Energy is the hidden link between a faraway war and everyday life: strikes on refineries move global diesel and fuel prices, which feed into transport, food and heating costs everywhere. How the world handles partial deals like an energy truce also sets the template for whether wars can be limited step by step or simply grind on.

background_read: Volodymyr Zelenskyy (Ukraine's president since 2019) has been asking Western allies for air-defense systems since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022. The war has followed a repeating winter pattern: Russia pounds power plants and heating systems to make civilian life unbearable, while Ukraine tries to shoot down as much as it can.

Russia is one of the world's largest oil exporters, and its refineries fuel both its economy and its military — which is why Ukraine targets them, and why strikes on Russian refineries can push up diesel prices far beyond the battlefield.

The 'energy ceasefire' idea borrows from an earlier partial deal: the Black Sea grain agreement, which allowed Ukraine to export food by ship while the war continued. Such partial deals can be a first step, but they usually break down unless both sides believe the cost of breaking them is higher than the gain.

The talks took place around the UN General Assembly (the annual meeting in New York where leaders of nearly every country speak). The Patriot system (an American-made ground-based interceptor) is the only weapon in Ukraine's arsenal that can reliably shoot down Russia's fast ballistic missiles — and global stocks are limited because several conflicts are competing for the same production lines.

perspectives.description: A working energy truce would protect civilians on both sides through the coldest months and could serve as a test case for wider negotiations. Zelenskyy is pairing it with a concrete ask — more Patriot interceptors — so the offer is not just words.

Nearly identical pledges were made only last week and collapsed within days, so a truce would mainly give Russia time to repair refineries and regroup. Critics also fear that any hint of easing sanctions would reward attacks on Ukrainian cities rather than stop them.

Partial agreements such as the Black Sea grain deal show that enemies can cooperate on narrow issues even mid-war, but they survive only while both sides see a net gain. Because Ukraine's drone campaign and Russia's winter strikes are each other's leverage, energy infrastructure has become a bargaining chip rather than a purely military target.

The decisive variables are weather, weapons and politics: whether Patriot supplies can be replenished, whether Washington keeps pressing Moscow, and whether November's US midterm elections change the pressure Trump applies. Without enforcement, the next 'energy ceasefire' may be announced and broken just as fast.
